Senses.Explanation: The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp is a thirty-fascicle compiled record of Chan teachers and their sayings. Chan authors cite, read, criticize, and identify the book as a documentary source; title occurrences are not assigned to the masters recorded inside it. The stored witnesses span 6 independent works and preserve the exact headword in the quoted Chinese. The gloss reports the shared deployment and leaves each surrounding case to its own recorded exchange.

Senses.Note: The exact headword has 104 occurrences in 28 allowed texts. Most belong to the book title treated in the second sense; the free phrase recurs with being unbroken, continuing the flame, succession, generations, ancestral portraits, and separate teaching regions. A complete concordance review found no independently attested hardware sense. A festival line about lamps and the moon reverses the graph order and therefore does not establish one.

Senses.Explanation: To continue the lineage lamps is to carry Chan succession from predecessor to successor and from generation to generation. Yongjue Yuanxian defines the governing lamp image in the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian: successive transmission is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and reveals things, and because its illumination can continue without end. His histories then call more than seventy generations an unbroken chain of linked lamps and describe them as linking the lamps while continuing the flame. Hanxiu Ruqian uses the phrase in memorial verses for succession after receiving his predecessor's blows and for two named lineage holders carrying the line in different regions. Zefeng Yue applies it to an ancestral portrait during a teaching-seat address. These uses concern public lineage continuity, not ordinary lamps physically fastened together.

Senses.Note: This is a different thing from lineage succession: it is a named thirty-fascicle text with a compiler, contents, prefaces, printing blocks, circulation history, and an abbreviated record title. The full title occurs 77 times in 13 allowed texts; the shorter title occurs once. The explicit referent label in the preferred target keeps the distinction visible without relying on capitalization alone.

The headword is a title in this row, so it supports the lineage-lamp explanation but does not buy free-phrase depth

Senses.Explanation: The book Linked-Lamp Essentials is a specific Chan compilation, not the act of continuing a lineage. In his self-preface, Huiweng Wuming says that he selected material from more than six hundred teachers, arranged encounters, questions and answers, comments on old and recent cases, and essential statements under each person's chapter, divided the work into thirty fascicles, and gave it this title. Li Yong's preface says the title was placed on the work and the blocks were carved for circulation. Yongjue Yuanxian later places Wuming's compilation among the five lamp records. A lineage biography records Wuming as its compiler, while Sichong's republication preface calls it the Linked-Lamp Record and recounts its printing history.

Senses.Explanation: The Essential Collection of the Linked Lamps is a lamp-history title, not a teaching phrase. Its own title heading names the work, while later lineage biographies repeatedly say that Huiweng Wuming compiled it and transmitted it in the monasteries. Those biographies use the book as evidence of Huiweng Wuming's editorial work and the continuation of recorded lineages; parallel retellings of that fact do not create additional senses.

Senses.Explanation: Luzu faces the wall names a recurrent case-action: when a visitor came, Luzu turned and faced the wall. Later masters repeatedly ask for its intent, answer with unrelated-looking phrases, reject proposed explanations, and compose verses under the case title. Later questioners repeatedly ask ‘what is the intent of Luzu facing the wall?’ Zifu Rubao answers that it has no connection; Huilin Hongji asks what there is to explain; Zhu'an Shigui answers with the five phases and celestial bodies. Verse collections preserve “Luzu faces the wall” as a case heading, while a later appraisal gives Luzu and Mazu's closed door twenty blows. These are public re-raisings of one remembered action, not descriptions of private contemplation.
